articleTitle: Management: Using the learning curve as a management tool: The learning curve can help in preparing cost reduction programs, pricing forecasts, and product development goals
abstract: In the fierce competition that shook the semiconductor industry in the 1950s, transistor and diode prices tumbled, along with more than a few managerial heads, as company after company discovered the importance of the learning curve. What this taught basically was this: As a manufacturer gains experience in making a product, he should be able to produce it more “cleverly,” more efficiently and in greater volume, and thus be in a position to cut prices. Successful companies applied the learning curve and survived. One way of applying the curve is to ensure volume production quickly by initially heavy investing in capital equipment.

articleTitle: Microprocessors get integrated sensors: Sensing devices and signal processing built into one silicon chip portend a new class of ‘smart’ sensors
abstract: Considers the development of silicon microsensors which can fit on the same chip with a microprocessor. Various sensor types are described, their fabrication presented and their possible applications pointed to.

articleTitle: Photovoltaics V: amorphous silicon cells: A highly homogeneous amorphous semiconductor material promises low-cost solar cells
abstract: Briefly describes the historical development of amorphous silicon, produced from a glow discharge in silane gas, which was found to be highly homogeneous and having very few defect states. This material at present is being investigated for low-cost solar cell production by the deposition of thin films onto a substrate because the manufacturing process is cheaper, less silicon is used per cell and the process is very suitable for mass production.

articleTitle: Solid state: VLSI with a vengeance: The Pentagon's very-high-speed integrated circuits project requires revolutionary advances in systems and IC technology
abstract: Discusses the Pentagon's very-high-speed integrated circuits project which requires revolutionary advances in systems and IC technology. The VHSIC program was initiated to develop VLSI signal processors with several hundred times higher speed and computing power than today's LSI devices. The planned processors must also consume less power and be smaller and more reliable. They are for use in military applications with no counterparts in commerce or industry-mainly real-time signal processors for weapons systems of the next decade. The goal of the program is pilot production in 1986 of processors containing 250000 gates, operating at clock speeds of at least 25 MHz, and performing several million to several billion operations per second. The gates would be fabricated by MOS or bipolar technology and have minimum dimensions of 0.5 to 0.8 μm. The required speed and circuit density would be obtained both by scaling down current LSI circuits-proportionately reducing such basic parameters as channel length, oxide thickness, and supply voltage-and by developing new types of system architecture and software.

articleTitle: Law enforcement: Shortcomings of radar speed measurement: It's based on sound principles, but present systems have practical limitations and may be misused
abstract: The accuracy of radar devices as they have been used to enforce speed laws on roads in the United States is being questioned. Well-publicized court rulings - such as last year's State of Florida v. Ana Aguilera ruling - have found radar speed readings inadmissible as legal evidence, because the radars were operated in such a way as to cast doubt on the accuracy of the readings.

Avionics computers of the 1990s are self-repairing, and they are so reliable that they remain operational despite multiple hardware or software failures. The pilot is excluded from the flight - stabilizing loop, since no human intervention could be swift or precise enough to handle the advanced airframes of the 1990s. The airframes are more fuel - efficient than previous models, but they are less stable and require the continuous action of super-reliable computers - and so the computers are as indispensible to flight as wings.

articleTitle: Computers/software: Words into action: I: Spoken advice can be recognized and converted to standard digital commands
abstract: Automatic speech recognition is entering a crucial phase. While users of the first systems are assessing the benefits and weighing them against costs, researchers are vigorously continuing to explore even more advanced systems. Development of the newer systems is not going to be easy.

articleTitle: Communications: Bell's echo-killer chip: Annoying echoes in two-way conversations via satellite are eliminated by using an inexpensive silicon circuit
abstract: A complete echo canceler on a single silicon integrated circuit is an economical solution to a persistent problem in long-distance communications: The echo of a caller's previously spoken words. This echo, if not completely eliminated is far more annoying on satellite circuits than on terrestrial circuits because of the increased transmission delay. The echo-canceler IC however, will make satellilte and terrestrial links comparable in quality. Satellite links, morever, are potentially cheaper than terrestrial systems. Such links have no expensive repeater stations and they are easier to rearrange when traffic patterns change.

articleTitle: Photovoltaics IV: Advanced materials: Both polycrystalline and tandem cells promise higher efficiencies than silicon
abstract: Considers the use of compound semiconductors for the fabrication of solar cells with high efficiency such as polycrystalline, tandem and single-crystal cells. The variety of compounds showing promise for this application are mentioned, as are several binary compound semiconductors which are presently under study. The low-cost processes being developed for the fabrication of solar cells are also briefly mentioned.

articleTitle: Photovoltaics III: Concentrators: Focusing the sun's rays, using cheap, long-lived optics, will be exploited in direct sunlight regions
abstract: Considers photovoltaic concentrating systems, indicating the problems inherent in their use which are, namely, ensuring that the systems are reliable and long-lived and reducing the costs of the optical and tracking components. The author also presents the US Department of Energy's cost goals for concentrating systems and indicates the progress made towards reaching these goals. Performance characteristics of operating systems are presented.

articleTitle: Telecommunications: NTIA: A small agency tackles large issues: The Carter-created National Telecommunications and Information Administration influences technical and social communications issues
abstract: As the U.S. expands from an industrial society to take on aspects of an information society, the National Telecommunications and Information Administration (NTIA), the President's advisor and spokesman on telecommunications and information, finds a growing range of issues in its territory: common carrier deregulation, international telecommunications, privacy in telecommunications, copyright and other intellectual property rights, the solar power satellite program, public television, and continuing education for the recertification of professional people, including electrical engineers in some states. With a relatively small staff of about 400 in the Department of Commerce, NTIA develops policies for the President and presents his policies to Congress, the Federal Communications Commission, state governments, international bodies, and other groups wrestling with regulation that affects telecommunications issues.

articleTitle: Power/energy: Cogeneration: An energy saver: This old and proven practice is even more attractive as the costs of primary fuels soar
abstract: Cogeneration — the production of electric power or mechanical shaft power in combination with a useful thermal energy supply - is becoming increasingly attractive to manufacturers, commercial establishments, residential consumers, and utilities because it offers a good return-on-investment possibility. Another advantage is that it increases the availability of reliable power in a utility blackout or natural disaster. Alternative fuels used in cogeneration systems can also reduce environmental pollutants.

articleTitle: Superconducting power cables: Both technological push and demand pull are needed to spur progress in superconducting, supercooled cables
abstract: The time is 1995. Three parallel underground 230-k V circuits, each with three identical superconducting ac cables " one for each phase " are carrying about 10 000 MW of electricity from an energy park into Philadelphia. The park is on the Susquehanna River some 106 km to the southwest. The route traverses farmland, suburban areas, and, in its last 10 km, a densely populated urban area. Helium refrigeration keeps the temperature within the cables at 6.5 to 8.5 K, enough to maintain superconductivity, or zero electrical dc resistance.

articleTitle: Communications and microwave: Orbit and spectrum congestion; tests for electronic mail; phone by light
abstract: Terrestrial and space communications have so crowded the spectrum available to satellites in geosynchronous orbit that saturation is threatened, and a search is under way for solutions to avert the interruption of services. Specialists estimate that unless corrective action is taken, there will be no room for new satellites by 1990, and the existing transmission frequency bands will be cluttered with interference.

articleTitle: Words into action II: A task-oriented system: Harpy is an experimental, continuous-speech recognition system that exploits a low-cost minicomputer
abstract: Discusses the Harpy experimental system using a low-cost minicomputer which is capable of automatic speech recognition with up to 98% accuracy when the vocabulary is restricted to 1011 words, and sentence structure limited to that used in the retrieval of abstracts of documents relating to computer technology. The recognition process of the system is described.

articleTitle: Computers: Bubbles take on disks: Application advances for bubble memories depend upon increased density and speed, standardization, and support circuitry
abstract: Now that magnetic bubble memories are on the market, we can expect a deluge of manufacturer reports on their applications and rosy future. It has already started to drizzle. The drizzle indicates that bubbles are competitive with floppy disks in small systems — 300 kb to 10 Mb of resident storage — and that the rivalry will spread to larger systems in the next decade.

articleTitle: Words into action III: A commercial system: Dynamic programming handles varying word lengths in this pioneer continuous-speech recognizer
abstract: Considers the Nippon Electric Co.'s DP-100 automatic continuous speech recognition system having an identification capability of approximately 100 words and aimed at application such as routing and inventory control in warehouses. The DP-100 design overcomes two serious handicaps which cause inaccuracies in automatic speech recognition systems, namely the variation in the rate at which words are spoken and the general problem of continuous speech recognition. The author gives details of the design and how these problems are overcome.

articleTitle: Photovoltaics II: Flat panels: Fixed-base silicon arrays are expected to exploit efficient, lightly doped cells
abstract: Presents a brief description of fixed-base flat silicon arrays and gives their advantages over tracking systems in particular climates. The author places great emphasis on silicon solar cells of the future with high performance characteristics allied with low fabrication costs which would be essential to make this a viable source of energy production. The structure of cells capable of achieving efficiencies of up to 21% is presented and further possible developments are indicated.

articleTitle: Electronics in medicine: Exploiting microprocessors; new hearing and seeing aids are developed; diagnostic imaging is refined
abstract: Advances in devices for the handicapped continue apace. In the very early experimental stages are implanted devices that stimulate the brain's visual cortex to enable blind persons to “see” and that stimulate the cochlea, or inner ear, to enable deaf persons to “hear.” Closer to commercial reality are a host of other devices. The behind-the-scenes star of virtually all is the microprocessor. It is rapidly opening doors to innovation, to versatility through redesign, and to cost-cutting.

A quiet revolution within the semiconductor industry has been threatening to displace the two leading technologies in commercial large-scale integration: the redoubtable bipolar process and the n-channel metal-oxide semiconductor (NMOS).

articleTitle: Electronics in medicine: How computers talk to the blind: Sightless computer programmers provide input by keyboard and are responded to by a synthetic speech unit
abstract: Describes how microcomputers which make synthetic speech feasible promise to open up job opportunities for the blind in fields hitherto closed to them. A prototype microcomputer-controlled voice generator which allows a computer to communicate by synthesised voice with the programmer is described. The programmer interacts with the computer by keyboard in the conventional manner.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: A secret that's no surprise
abstract: A number of observers have recently expressed chagrin that Japanese manufacturers have moved into a position where they are claiming superiority in quality and productivity of high technology products over those of other advanced countries, including the U.S. To seasoned Japan-watchers, however, it is not a surprise.

articleTitle: Communications: Radio goes underground: Communicating in mine tunnels has been taken seriously by radio and microwave engineers only in the last decade
abstract: Considers underground radio techniques for communications in mines and underground mass transportation systems. Development of this new science is presented, serious research in the field of underground communication having only started about ten years ago, and the problems encountered and the appropriate solutions are given.

articleTitle: Communications: LSI helps telephones go digital: Low-cost, high-density chips accelerate the digital design of switching systems, terminals, and networks
abstract: Considers the advent of LSI devices for applications in the telecommunication industry leading to the changeover from analogue to fully digital networks. The importance of microelectronics in terms of reliability, cost-effectiveness and operation are discussed.

articleTitle: Power/energy: Managing switching arcs: Plasma physics research tells us how to dynamically control arcs in high-power circuit breakers
abstract: A new respect for electric arcs has developed among plasma physics researchers, and it is pointing the rugged way to gas-blast circuit breakers that can handle higher voltages. Arcs used to be looked upon as a nuisance that had to be extinguished, like a fire, as soon as possible. Now, the electric arc is regarded as a dynamic, controllable, and vital part of a circuit breaker.

articleTitle: 'Collision-proof' airspace: Reducing the risk of midair collisions is the goal of an air-traffic control system proposed by the FAA
abstract: Airline Flight 66 from Los Angeles has just entered the busy New York terminal control area on an afternoon in September 1989. The jetliner's approach will carry it across New Jersey just south of Newark, with a left turn up the Hudson River, a wide right turn over Yonkers, N. Y., and a final turn and approach over Flushing Bay onto Runway 22 at LaGuardia Airport.

articleTitle: Home communications I: Teletext and viewdata: Text and graphics are broadcast or transmitted over telephone wires to the home television receiver
abstract: Discusses teletext and viewdata generally, outlines the differences between them, their flexibility, common display features, receivers and the extra services possible. Also the systems in public service in Britain and other countries are discussed.

articleTitle: Optical fiber systems: Low-loss links: Long-wavelength intercity telecommunications increase repeater spacing and promise low cost
abstract: Reports of optical fiber system research and development, in Europe point to the following: (1) Low-loss systems operating in the 1100 to 1600-nm waveband show promise of high performance with long repeater spacings. (2) A strong effort is under way to develop wideband switched networks as an economical and competitive alternative to CATV networks. (3) Fiber links may be used to provide digital pathways to business premises to service a large private automatic branch exchange (PABX), but the real impact will come only with video services. (4) No major failure have been reported for optical fiber systems; users find them simple to install, rugged, and less demanding in duct space. (5) The first generation of fiber systems, now entering service, offer the same quality and cost of service as present telecommunication systems. These points are discussed in this paper.

articleTitle: Communications: How Diana touched the moon: An impromptu band of Army radio experimenters established man's first contact with outer space in 1946
abstract: Describes how an impromptu band of US army radio experimenters established man's first contact with outer space in 1946 by bouncing a radar signal off the Moon.

In a world shrunken by intercontinental communications and jet travel, one can hardly talk of a national or regional electrotechnology. Yet, the needs of Western Europe in two key areas alone — communications and transportation — differ from those of other developed regions. There are several reasons for this. West European population density is among the highest in the world. Big cities are close together. Many languages are spoken in what is a relatively small region. And energy resources, aside from those in Norway and Britain, are limited. West Europe, as a whole, imports 60 to 70 percent of its primary energy, and in some of its smaller countries, that level is even higher. Yet, the region consumes energy intensively. One source with the European Economic Community estimates that West Europe, like Japan, consumes four to five times more energy per square kilometer than the United States does. This helps account for the region's high standard of living, which is maintained largely through the export of manufactured goods.

articleTitle: Computers: Data privacy: The European community grapples with protecting individual rights in the midst of rampant computer progress
abstract: The matter of invasion of privacy has become a touchy issue in the computer age, and Europe is moving to resolve questions of human rights with uniform legal guarantees. The emerging branch of law is called data protection. Already, some people are questioning whether the law will ever be able to catch up with reality. For example, the notion of `data bank', which appears in some laws, is already becoming inadequate; it is now possible to manipulate data instantaneously without a permanent record. As a result, French law now uses the term `data treatment'. A further example: with networks and intelligent terminals for data processing, rules intended originally for specialists now must address the public at large. For this very reason, an ongoing dialogue between lawyers and data-processing experts is essential.

articleTitle: An electronic advisor/companion: Computers able to function as personal consultants require breakthroughs in the field of artificial intelligence
abstract: Some people are going through life with an electronic “companion.” No bigger than a portable radio, it “grows up” with a person, learns his or her habits and personality traits, picks up knowledge of the person's business affairs, and learns enough law, medicine, and finance to render simple advice in these areas. Expert consultant systems like these are being used by pace-setting physicians, scientists, and lawyers in the 1990s.

articleTitle: Solid state: Thyristors on the move: New applications are seen in power converters and inverters for trains, industrial motors, and HVDC
abstract: Thryistor technology has developed rapidly in Europe since its introduction, largely because about one-fifth of the electric power generated is consumed as dc power, and electric trains are so widely used.

articleTitle: Avionics: All digital jets on the horizon: The Boeing 767 is the most talked about new airliner in years because of its ambitious use of digital avionics
abstract: Digital avionics are used sparingly on today's jetliners, but they will completely displace analog systems on next-generation airliners, due for commercial operation in 1982. The big question is: Will it be worth the effort?

articleTitle: Innovation in the factory: Energy-efficient processes are sought, and the computer is used to merge design and fabrication functions
abstract: The same innovative designs and technological advances that have pushed paper-based office systems into the arms of computer vendors moved some industries closer to the automated factory last year. The goals of manufacturing and industrial engineers were to conserve energy, reduce costs, and upgrade productivity and product quality.

articleTitle: A tribute: Patrick E. Haggerty: Engineer and visionary: His colleagues remember him with affection and respect, a persistent, persuasive manager who was an inspiration to his associates
abstract: For six years after the invention of the transistor in 1948, the development lay commercially neglected. The U.S. military was interested in applying it, but most commercial and consumer engineers resisted any changeover from vacuum tubes. At Texas Instruments in Dallas, the story was different. Patrick Eugene Haggerty, then the company's executive vice president, had caught an early vision of the transistor's potential, and it helped alter the course of commercial electronics.

articleTitle: Consumer electronics: Intelligent television receivers; personal computers proliferate; cable TV expands
abstract: Increasing design-effort continues to be invested in conversion of the television receiver to a home information center. The improvements being designed into the IV set range from processor-controlled tuners in the receiver to viewdata and teletext decoders for upcoming data-bank services.

articleTitle: Instrumentation: Digital storage oscilloscopes: Digital scopes may evolve like the digital multimeter, offering data-capture, transfer, and processing in addition to present capabilities
abstract: The storage oscilloscope has entered a new phase of development that opens the door to new applications for this electronic instrument. No longer does it have just storage and display features. The newer digital storage models also provide data acquisition and processing capabilities. This means that oscilloscopes can be used in automatic test setups. Even in stand-alone applications, the processing digital oscilloscope eliminates the need for highly skilled personnel to interpret the waveform measurements.

articleTitle: Sociotechnology: Engineers and politics: Seven survival commandments: A catechism to help engineers champion technology through the morass of political processes in the U.S.
abstract: Most religions were developed in a much simpler era than this one. Their commandments give guidance on the relationships among individual people, but they are not of much help when it comes to relations among organizations. This is an era in which technologies change and cause changes in organizations, which in turn develop new relations to one another.

articleTitle: Solid state: Four targets of VLSI: Medical electronics, telecommunications, terminals, and scientific computers are candidates for its early application
abstract: When very-large-scale integration becomes a commercial reality, the chips will be used first as custom circuits in at least four application areas: medical electronics, telecommunications for the office and elsewhere, personal intelligent terminals, and scientific computers. Manufacturers in these industries have finally started to define what functions should be integrated on single monoliths.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Saving energy by design
abstract: “White goods” consume a relatively small percentage of the total residential electric power in U.S. homes. Refrigerators, freezers, room air conditioners, ranges and microwave ovens, clothes washers and dryers, and dishwashers together probably account for about one third of electric power consumption in the home. The rest goes for water and space heating, lighting, and to operate low-power entertainment and convenience devices.

As Spectrum's editors began the research that culminated in this annual review of a dozen major areas of technology, it quickly became clear that there would be not just one theme that would predominate, but at least two major ones. At the outset, it was evident that very large scale integration would be one topic of interest in a number of the sections of the issue. Its thread is found in several of the applications sections — computers and solid-state devices of course, but also communications, military and aerospace, and instrumentation.

articleTitle: Satellite communications II: Television for everyone: Low-cost Earth stations that can select from a broad menu of satellite broadcasts are sought
abstract: Sometime in the 1980s-perhaps as early as 1984-television programs relayed by satellite will be received by small, inexpensive Earth stations mounted on the houses of viewers or antennas in their local communities. Viewers will be able to choose from at least five new TV channels and, in some areas, as many as 20 or 30. The projected European satellite broadcasting service will use geostationary satellites to relay TV and sound signals from Earth transmitters to Earth receivers. Unlike conventional satellite communications systems, the new TV satellite system will not use large, expensive receiver antennas, but small (about 1 m diameter fixed parabolic dishes on buildings.

articleTitle: Politics of technology: U.S. technological progress: Alternative approaches: Technical developments might best be served by modifying existing agencies or by legislation, rather than by creating a new agency
abstract: A National Engineering Foundation within the Federal government was recently proposed by Bruno Weinschei, president of the Weinschel Engineering Co. in Gaithersburg, Md., to help increase innovation and productivity in the United States (Spectrum, February, pp. 58-60). Allen B. Rosenstein, professor of engineering at the University of California, Los Angeles, then suggested a different type of Federal agency - a National Professions Foundation (Spectrum, August, pp. 41-43). Meanwhile, a National Technology Foundation has been proposed in Congress. In this article, F. Karl Willenbrock discusses alternatives to the new agency approach.

articleTitle: The global video conference: Both user acceptance and economics block the widespread use of video conferencing
abstract: Every major corporation in the United States with more than two divisions dispersed hundreds of miles apart has a video conference system at its sites. The video conference room has become as much a part of corporate life as the boardroom - a tool made feasible by the growth of satellite business communications and one deemed essential in 1990 for efficient conduct of a company's businesses.

articleTitle: Transportation: The promise of maglev: Tests will continue with a high-speed vehicle and track incorporating a linear motor
abstract: A magnetically levitated railway vehicle that would whisk 200 to 600 passengers between cities at up to 400 km/h is being developed in West Germany. The government has put its research and development money on a train that moves without touching the tracks. This paper discusses the advantages of such a system and its construction. These include track flexibility, linear motor formed by vehicle and track, sensors to control vehicle suspension, and linear generator for on-board power. The vehicle's economic competitiveness and favourable energy use are indicated.

articleTitle: Instruments get smarter: Innovative digital design techniques lead to more intelligent, versatile, and communicative instruments
abstract: A new wave of instruments is promised for the new decade. The impetus is the growing infusion of digital design techniques in test and measurement equipment.

articleTitle: An electric car in every garage: This optimistic goal is far off; progress toward it hinges on high-performance batteries
abstract: After a decade of development, the electric vehicle is in modest supply in the United States in December 1990. Hundreds of thousands - some say about a million - are operating on roads. For the buyer, the choice is among two- and four-passenger cars, some vans, and some trucks - but all limited to about 150 km on a 6- to 10-hour nighttime battery recharge. For most families, the electric is a second car or an auxiliary vehicle, for urban and suburban driving. Many utilities encourage nighttime charging of batteries by providing lower electricity rates then. Nights have traditionally been the lowest demand periods for electric energy. The electric vehicles meet all the Federal motor vehicle safety standards. They can accelerate from 0 to 50 km/h in about 8 seconds, and cruise at 90 km/h. They can merge smoothly with other traffic on the road and seem to have no problem operating in - 10°C in northern areas.

It may be the 21st Century, but Monday morning's rush hour in the big city is as hectic as ever. Rail commuters prepare to disembark, poised to race through the underground maze of newsstands, shops, and passageways in the busy midtown subway station. Some scurry to catch connecting trains, other scout for exit signs marking the route to the surface. Moving somewhat hesitantly, yet unnoticed by the tide of humanity, is a blind man wearing glasses. He has no cane, no guide dog or escort. Instead, he is equipped with an artificial vision system designed to provide a useful level of mobility.

articleTitle: Communications: WARC plots spectrum use: The World Administrative Radio Conference sought accommodating solutions between developed and third world states
abstract: Take a global conference held once in 20 years, add 1800 delegates from 142 countries, put 10 000 proposals on the agenda, and allow 11 weeks to reach decisions. This was the challenge facing the World Administrative Radio Conference last Sept. 24 to Dec. 5 in Geneva, Switzerland, and the results were perhaps predictable: Many broad decisions were made, but the details of implementing were mostly put off to another day.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Advice on how to run a railroad
abstract: In December 1979, Spectrum published the article “The LIRR: a system riding troubled tracks” and solicited the advice of readers on improvements that might be made in the design or operation of the system.

articleTitle: Nuclear power: TMI: An insider's viewpoint: Texas Instrument's Patrick E. Haggerty, a member of the President's Commission on TMI, reviews the nuclear outlook
abstract: As one of only three engineers on the 12-member President's Commission on the Accident at Three Mile Island, Patrick E. Haggerty saw the panel's broad citizen makeup as a blessing in analyzing the nation's worst nuclear reactor accident. In support of this view, he points to a major flaw uncovered by the investigation — poor design of control room displays — and observes:

articleTitle: Computers: Electronics aids the athlete: Biomechanical systems are useful in human factors engineering, and in the design of sports equipment and prosthetic devices
abstract: Olympic athletes intent on breaking world records are turning to sophisticated software programs and high-speed computer systems to plot their performances and find ways to improve them. The software and computer systems analyze slow-motion movies of an athlete's movements and estimate bone and muscle stresses in relation to the movements. From this information, it is possible to postulate some optimum movements that might help an athlete break an existing record.

articleTitle: Best bits: Applications of microprocessors: Low-cost nuclear safety
abstract: Existing control-room simulators for nuclear reactors can only reproduce a nuclear accident; their internal computers are not powerful enough to predict what happens if the variables change. However, such a predictive simulator might be built of multiple microprocessors, participants at a jointly sponsored IEEE/NRC electrotechnology conference in Washington, D.C., have suggested. The system might work many times faster than even a high-speed scientific computer.

articleTitle: Other meetings: Series SE3000 lightweight, instrummentation recorders
Politics of technology: OTA: Congress' own think tank: After seven years of controversy, the Office of Technology Assessment is shunning the spotlight to survive in a ‘political jungle’
abstract: Wouldn't it be a great idea to place a microscopic chip in commercial explosives so that, following a terrorist bombing, law enforcement officials could trace the explosive used to its last legal sale? Wouldn't that help to control terrorists?

articleTitle: II: Creating a market for Prestel
abstract: For pt.I see ibid., vol.17, no.3, p.26-27, 30-2 (1980). Many interdependent problems are being tackled to create a favorable market for the British Prestel viewdata system. The United Kingdom has two contrasting traditions in the control of information media. On the one hand, there is the open market tradition of newspaper, magazine, and book publishing. On the other hand, there is the tradition in radio and television of control by government-appointed public bodies (the British Broadcasting Corp. and the Independent Broadcasting Authority). These bodies concern themselves with the content of the transmissions. For this reason, and because of the limited capacity of the radio frequency spectrum, broadcast radio and television cannot offer an open market in the provision and consumption of information. To create an efficient market, a number of conditions should be met: there should be a sound legal basis for transactions; information buyers and sellers should have easy access to the data bank; sellers should not be restricted in defining their product nor in setting prices; buyers and sellers should be able to determine the amount of information to be sold; and, rewards for the seller and credit for the buyer should be ensured.

articleTitle: Microprocessors: Beating an electronic opponent is a challenge: But the road from the concept of an intelligent game to the final product is both challenging and tortuous
abstract: Got an idea for an intelligent electronic game? It will take more than convincing a game manufacturer to bring it to fruition, it took Gary O'Hara and Tim Shane seven years before their highly successful backgammon game, Gammonmaster, landed on department store shelves. The long turnaround wasn't due only to engineering problems, but rather because of such uncertain factors as cost/performance trade-offs, market acceptance-, and competition from other game vendors and other television video games.

articleTitle: Automotive electronics: Microcomputers hit the road: U.S. automakers are turning to digital electronic controls to boost fuel economy and reduce pollution
abstract: By 1981, most new cars made in the U.S. will use microcomputer-based engine controls to increase gas mileage while reducing exhaust emissions. Microcomputer-based controls — systems that optimize ignition timing and air/fuel ratio, for example — are the automakers' way of meeting Federal requirements in the 1980s to increase fuel economy and reduce pollution. Electronic engine controls arc still too expensive, however, to be used in all cars.

articleTitle: Consumer telephone I: A switch to electronics: Telephone systems will go completely electronic as reed relays are displaced by digital electronic switching
abstract: Discusses the changeover to digital electronic switching happening in many countries especially in Western Europe as reed relays are replaced in telephone systems. The progress of the French, Swedish, Italian, West German and British are outlined.

articleTitle: Power/energy: Low-head hydro power: Small may be beautiful but, so far the economics for small-scale hydroelectric sites cloud a bright potential
abstract: Large-scale hydroelectric generation remains one of the cheapest forms of electricity in the United States, but the best sites with high heads (the height of the water drop available) have been used. The remaining low-head sites have seemed far less economical. With the rise in oil prices, however, many of these low-head sites are being reexamined.

articleTitle: Air safety: The Federal Aviation Administration under scrutiny: The U.S. Congress and others have ideas about improving air safety that include restructuring the FAA and altering its charter
abstract: It has been a rough couple of years for the Federal Aviation Administration. “Discovered” by Congressional committees, consumer groups, and blue-ribbon panels, the agency has come under a degree of public scrutiny that other Government bodies long have endured, but that the FAA managed to sidestep. For years, it operated much like the Federal Bureau of Investigation once did, as the unquestioned authority in its field. Now. its methods, aims, and charter are being challenged. Much of this attention was piqued by two air tragedies — a midair collision between an airliner and a light plane over San Diego in 1978 and a DC-10 crash in Chicago in 1979. The combined death toll from the accidents was 417 people. Further, there has been a recent series of FAA computer failures that have raised the risk of more midair collisions.

articleTitle: Consumer telephone III: Mixing new with old: An interfacing scheme for analog and digital systems features modular architecture
abstract: For pt.II see ibid., vol.17, no.3, p.38-40 (1980). A telephone switching system that embodies a unique design philosophy is now into its third year of service. The AXE-10, a digital stored-program-control (SPC) system, is made up of functional modules in individual hardware and software configurations. They are interconnected via strictly defined hardware and software interfaces. This building block principle makes the system generally applicable on all levels of the telephone network and permits smooth introduction of new parts into the system without changing its concept. Also, handling and operation of the system are easier as compared to the monolithic-type systems of earlier generation. The physical design, also modular in nature, using a magazine concept, has reduced testing, shipping and installation times, and at the same time increases reliability by a sizable reduction of interconnection contact points.

articleTitle: Careers: We look at ourselves: A leisure-time portrait: Here's a profile of the IEEE member, constructed from Spectrum interviews and a comprehensive survey
abstract: He is 40 years old, holds a degree from a four-year college, and is married to a woman who has attended college. He is a family man who is likely to stay married — divorce is only an outside possibility. His family income is $32 356 a year. He owns a home worth $72 684, has two cars, and more leisure possessions than the average citizen.

When the edict came from above to cut his payroll by 50 percent, the chief engineer was faced with a dilemma. Which of his modest three person team should he let go? He had recently urged Smith, his senior man, to join him from another department within the company, specifically to prepare for a contract which, ultimately, was awarded to a competitor. Smith, age 42, was earning $36 000. Brent, on the other hand, was in the middle of an ongoing project that could enhance both the company's income and its reputation. Brent had five years of solid experience in the area of his project, was 26 years old, and earned $22 000. Jones was the newest member of the department — a bright, enthusiastic recent graduate. She was earning $14 000.

articleTitle: A special report: And if hasn't been, at least not yet. A study of 11 wanted projects requiring technical, economic, or institutional breakthroughs before fruition is possible
abstract: Engineers and scientists are accustomed to looking at the world as it is and coming up with solutions to ever more complex problems, but for a host of wanted projects that have potential for improving the quality of life, fruition seems elusive.

articleTitle: Satellite communications I: ESA at the crossroads: Projects for the 1980s at the space agency include satellite launches and a space platform
abstract: After a decade of national and transnational communications satellite programs, Europe is at the crossroads. It will move in this decade from the preoperational phase to the use of systems responding to its own needs. It is about to become competitive with the United States and Canada in this field. Five flight units of the European Communications Satellite are being built by European industry, with the first to be orbited by an Ariane launcher in October 1981. These satellites are to be used for carrying long-distance telephone traffic within Europe and for a television interchange service. In addition, ESA is committed to launching three maritime communications satellites. This decade will also see the development by European nations of a space platform that could hold a range of payloads for future communications needs.

articleTitle: Program preview: Electro '80: Microprocessors star: Opening May 13 in Boston, the 3-day meeting features three ‘blocks’ of technical sessions daily
abstract: Instrumentation and the microprocessor have leading roles in the technical drama that will unfold May 13–15 at Electro '80, but the supporting cast is impressive. Thirty-four technical and professional sessions arc planned. They will focus on new trends and applications in digital systems, memories, high-temperature electronics, communications, fiber optics, and more.

articleTitle: Careers: We look at ourselves: The EE student: A picture of today's electrical engineering students emerges from interviews with 16 of them, aged 20 to 24, at 10 U.S. colleges
abstract: Carrying five-color pens in the pockets of their Oxford shirts, they wear calculators on their belts and have oscilloscopes in their dorm rooms. They are great with numbers and can fix anything that has a battery, but when it comes to putting words on paper, they are helpless. They are conservative, cautious, and not inclined to take risks. They are introverted and don't socialize much - in fact, they're more comfortable talking to computers than people. In 10 or 15 years, they will settle down contentedly in middle-class suburbia.

Sometime in the 1990s a design engineer sits down at a personal computer that does more than paint pretty pictures graphically or run canned application programs: It can support computer programs that realistically model designs in an interactive way, defined totally by the designer, not by a computer programmer.

articleTitle: Politics of technology: Proposal: A National Engineering Foundation: Would it not help to halt the slide in U.S. productivity and its loss in share of world markets?
abstract: Let's face it: The United States economy is sputtering. The U.S. position in world trade has deteriorated. Its ability to compete in the export market or against imports has decreased. Industrial investment in targeted basic research and applied research leading to improvements in productivity or major new markets is discouraged by regulatory and tax policies.

articleTitle: Politics of technology: National Professions Foundation: An idea whose time has come?: With U.S. leadership in technology and the professions declining and the very quality of life in jeopardy, an NPF is recommended to remedy the situation
abstract: A National Engineering Foundation within the Federal government was recently proposed by Bruno Weinschel, president of the Weinschel Engineering Co. in Gaithersburg, Md., to help increase innovation and productivity in the United States (Spectrum, February, pp. 58-60). In this article, Allen B. Rosenstein proposes a different type of Federal agency - a National Professions Foundation.

articleTitle: Technology and society: Nuclear power pervades the public interest while alternate solutions are investigated
abstract: It could go down in technical history books as the Year of Pessimism. Many people in the world saw technology in 1979 as a demon rather than a useful genie to mankind. From the nuclear accident at Three Mile Island to scarce energy supplies and fear of a falling Skylab, the public perception of technology was gloomy.

With all the fanfare about high-level languages and concurrent processes in the technical literature, it is interesting to note that programmers at the Megadata Corp, of Bohemia, N.Y., have put in about seven man-years on a 40 000-word program written entirely in assembly language — and were they to do it over, they say they would still do it mostly in assembly language.

Following are selected references on each of the Special Reports to aid readers who wish to investigate the subject further. These references are not offered as a complete representation of the work done in any of the fields, but as a starting place for research in the topics. Readers wishing more information will find that 6368395following the footnotes” in works listed here will lead to reading matter in almost any desired facet of the topics.

articleTitle: Best bits: Applications of microprocessors: Aiding the disadvantaged
abstract: About four million children of school age have communication disabilities, according to Dr. Haig Kafafian, head of the Cybernetics Research Institute at Upsala College in New Jersey. Many would benefit from relatively inexpensive home communication aids. He believes the cost can be brought down with microprocessor-driven interfaces.

articleTitle: Aerospace: Europe gets aboard the Shuttle: The European Space Agency's Spacelab is making the dream of research in space come true
abstract: When Spacelab goes into Earth orbit two years from now, more than radically new hardware and improved methods for handling it will be at stake, it will also mark the start of an international scientific effort in which manned experiments will range from pure research in physics and other sciences to materials processing in space.

articleTitle: Careers: We look at ourselves: The design engineer: An introspective look at the personal and professional attributes of today's designers, gleaned from interviews with several of them
abstract: There is a design engineer in every one of us. Sand castles, Tinker Toys, and Erector sets were the media for our first creations. In time, electronic hobby kits added to the fascination. We began building the projects described in the pamphlets, until we were no longer satisfied with copying someone else's design. After a few failures, often spectacular, the day finally came when the lights flashed, the buzzer squawked, and the fuse didn't blow!

articleTitle: Software: The Russian algorithm: A second look: What was labeled a breakthrough in linear programming seems now to be largely of theoretical importance
abstract: It was too good to be true. News reports last fall indicated that the world of mathematics was being “rocked” by a Russian mathematician's discovery of shortcut solutions to decisionmaking problems common in business and industry — so-called linear programming problems that sometimes require weeks or months of computer time to solve, or could even take thousands of years of computer time.

articleTitle: Best bits: Applications of microprocessors: The `four-cylinder’ Caddy
abstract: How do you save gasoline and cut exhaust pollutants with an eight-cylinder Cadillac? It will be easy with the 1981 models, General Motor says. They will have as standard equipment a microcomputer that will allow the engine to use four, six, or all eight cylinders, as needed. GM's Cadillac Division says the cars will give 30 mi/gal on the highway at 55 mi/h.

articleTitle: Careers: We look at ourselves: Young EEs on their way up: From round-table discussions, a profile emerges of successful engineers and how they view their work
abstract: Considers various aspects of the work of electrical engineers, their criteria and motives for working and their valuable contributions towards the western world's property.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Helping the younger world
abstract: We of the developed world are now talking of helping the nations to whom technology is an attractive but unfamiliar tool - helping them to exploit technology while avoiding adverse consequences related thereto. The challenge is a large one. More than 70 of the present United Nations member states were territories under colonial rule when the UN was founded; most of them, in addition to others, fall into the lesser-developed category.

articleTitle: Spactral lines: Good news amid the bad
abstract: The beginning of a new decade invariably prompts forecasters to look ahead in a 10-year “bite.” Sociologists, economists, and laymen alike enjoy the challenge of identifying each decade by characteristics which are at best simplistic and at worst erroneous. Were the “Gay '90s” really that merry?

articleTitle: Home communications III: Videotext standards: International experts are hard at work defining standards to interface new services with divergent systems
abstract: For pt.II see ibid., vol.17, no.3, p.29 (1980). Eight international organizations are negotiating new international standards for transmitting data from computer banks to home TV receivers. Two general objectives are common to these discussions: facilitation of the international exchange of data and agreement on TV standards that would lead to production of a universal receiver. Proposals are under consideration in the Conference of European Posts and Telecoms Administration (CEPT) and in the International Telegraph and Telephone Consultative Committee (CCITT) on coding schemes, page format, and user protocols. Six other international groups are looking into comparable issues. The British viewdata system, Prestel, is providing the first technical data on a commercially operating system from the standpoints of both the user and the information provider.

articleTitle: Best bits: Applications of microprocessors: Switching to firmware
abstract: A father-and-son team of automotive engineers, Ervin and Michael Leshner, who have been voted 1979 Inventors of the Year by the American Society of Inventors, are working to produce prototypes of an engine-control device that would increase auto fuel efficiency at low installed cost. One question the Leshners face is at what point to convert their present 60 component control board of resistors and analog and digital ICs to a microprocessor-driven version containing about a quarter of the components and costing 40 percent less. Convert they must to meet their goal of a $150 retail price for an installed unit, but they are in no hurry to do so until they have produced between 1000 and 10 000 units.

articleTitle: Consumer telephone II: France goes digital: Low noise, switching versatility, and a reduction in A/D and D/A conversions result
abstract: For pt.I see ibid., vol.17, no.3, p.36-7 (1980). Since 1960, subscriber lines in France have become 100% automated. Digital conversion is increasing steadily and 30% of switching lines ordered in 1976 were digital. The advantages are low noise, switching versatility and a reduction in A/D and D/A conversion.

articleTitle: Power: Britain's fast breeder: The Dounreay test reactor experience has instilled confidence in its designers to press for commercialization
abstract: Discusses the Dounreay test reactor experience which has instilled confidence in its designers to press for commercialization. The test experience is based on the Dounreay test reactor (60 MW) and a prototype fast breeder (600 MW). The safety features designed into the prototype fast-breeder reactor include: Natural circulation to deal with fission product decay heat. It appears to be more than adequate to dissipate such heat. Natural feedback phenomena which would shut down the reactor from full power in the event of a mean coolant temperature rise over 620°C. No significant energetic fuel coolant interaction in the event of fuel meltdown has been found in a wide range by experiments. Acoustic waveguide devices to give indication of boiling in a few milliseconds and a triangulation technique to locate the point of boiling.

articleTitle: Standards: Why parts ‘fit’: The role of IEC: The International Electrotechnical Commission is busier than ever on the eve of its 75th anniversary
abstract: A Japanese engineer designs miniature fuses guided by international standards. A chief engineer of an Australian power utility places an order in the United States for overhead-line insulators knowing that they will be compatible with his installations. A U.S. communications engineer is operating a new radio transmitter knowing that he is protected by strict safety regulations against radiation, implosion and explosion, and fire. A Swiss biomedical engineer designs an improved X-ray diagnosis system using the latest international standards. A Detroit automotive engineer employs hermetically sealed nickel-cadmium cells in a prototype automobile battery knowing that the cells were manufactured in Japan according to published performance standards.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: They said it couldn't be done ... or can it?
abstract: The American public, as well as the citizens of other advanced nations, seems to have a love-hate relationship with technology.

articleTitle: Automobiles: Detroit plans a comeback: Billions of dollars are at stake in U.S. auto makers' catch-up battle with small, fuel-efficient imports
abstract: “Never in its history has Detroit been faced with so many problems.” Spectrum said that in November 1977 in a special issue on the automobile. Now, just three years later, U.S. automobile manufacturers look back to 1977 with fond memories of the good old days. As James McDonald, president to be of General Motors, put it at a recent meeting in Michigan: “Until Spring of '79, we couldn't build enough large cars. After Spring of '79, we couldn't build enough small cars.”

articleTitle: Energy: Solar ‘shift’ at SERI: The still young Solar Energy Research Institute is training its sights on short-term objectives
abstract: Emerging from an administrative shake-up and a shift in planning, the U.S. Government's leading solar research center no longer sees solar power as far off in the nation's future. “Solar is important right now,” says Denis Hayes, the new director of the Solar Energy Research Institute (SERI) in Golden, Colo.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Engineering education under fire: II
abstract: In a previous column, August, p. 19, we reviewed the concerns about the engineering educational process, giving particular notice to the situation in the U.S. We observed that the following issues are of greatest concern to U.S. educators: (1) poor equipment, (2) low graduate enrollents, (3) disproportionate enrollment of non-U.S. students, particularly at the graduate level, (4) low academic salaries, and (5) a need for enhanced cooperation between academia and industry.

articleTitle: Power/energy: Power for the '30s: A challenge for Western Europe: There is a way for Europe to make itself energy-independent. But is there a will?
abstract: Meeting Western Europe's power needs through the year 2000 will require new technology, a high level of international cooperation, and extensive application of mature technology. The new technology will be primarily nuclear, with emphasis on fast breeder reactors. International cooperation will be needed both in developing commercially feasible breeder reactors and in distributing the additional electricity that will become available. As for mature technology, further advances may be expected in such fields as pumped water storage.

At a recent annual technical meeting of one of IEEE's largest and most prestigious societies, several hundred attendees convened in an evening session in which several experts were about to discuss the status and future of a key electronics technology.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Engineering education under fire
abstract: Inflation and low industrial productivity have caused a sharpening of the perennial criticisms to which the engineering educational process is subjected. In the U.S., for example, the prevailing issues are (1) poor equipment, (2) low graduate enrollments, (3) disproportionate enrollment of non-nationals, particularly at the graduate level, (4) low academic salaries, and (5) a need for enhanced cooperation between academia and industry.

articleTitle: Sharper `eyes' for star gazers [a new submillimeter-wavelength radio receiver]
abstract: The radio astronomy receiver built at the European Space Research and Technology Center allows astronomers to study intergalactic molecules that emit radio signals of submillimeter wavelength. The receiver is basically a heterodyne frequency analyzer for detecting weak microwave signals of about 10<sup>-20</sup> W at 200 GHz to 400 GHz. Incoming signals are mixed with the signal from a local oscillator and downconverted to a lower frequency that can be amplified with low noise. The amplified signal is fed to a spectrometer, a bank of filters, and a minicomputer that yield the power spectra of received signals.

In the search for a new catalyst, Jay's group has narrowed the possibilities to A and B. Data, possibly erroneous, show B as the choice. But Jay, his whole group, and his boss (a catalyst expert) are certain A is better. His boss tells Jay to make up false data and write a report favoring catalyst A. What would you do in Jay's situation?

articleTitle: Cheap electricity from French tides: The sea has demonstrated both friendly and adverse effects during the 14-year history of the Saint Malo plant
abstract: Presents an overview of the Saint Mao tidal power electricity generating plant giving technical details of construction and operation. Operational experience over the last fourteen years is also presented.

articleTitle: Meeting preview: Wescon '80: Electronics at Disneyland: Anaheim will be the scene of high technology disclosures
abstract: “Electronics, the Magic Kingdom” is the theme of Wescon '80, the West Coast's annual convention and exhibition of electronics wizardry. The three-day event, starting Sept. 16, takes place at the Anaheim Convention Center in California, with the magic of Disneyland just across the road.

articleTitle: Electrotechnology is a ‘prime mover’: Electronic engine controls save fuel; battery cars are tested; automated ‘group rapid transit’ is funded
abstract: Saving fuel, reducing pollution, and improving safety and reliability are the driving forces behind transportation developments today.

articleTitle: Spectral lines: Good news amid the bad, part II
abstract: In a previous column, we took note of the gloomy forecasts for the 1980s, encompassing energy shortages, inflation, more crowded cities, inadequate job opportunities, drug abuse, violence and vandalism, along with a decreasing respect for property and human life. We noted that the wide application of technology and a more broadly educated populace had generated increased expectations among various segments of society. When not all these expectations are fulfilled, as they cannot be, the societal institutions are perceived by the public as ultimately responsible.

articleTitle: Electronics in medicine: RF therapy for malignancy: Heating of malignant tissues (hyperthermia) by RF radiation presents a new tool in the arsenal of weapons against cancer
abstract: Radio frequency radiation has become a promising new weapon against cancer. Medical researchers around the world report that the use of such radiation to heat malignant tissue to the hyperthermic range (42 to 43.5°C) appears to be a safe and efficient means for either destroying the cancer cells or making them more susceptible to other forms of treatment.

articleTitle: Electromagnetic hazards: RF radiation: Biological effects: Sharp controversy over the effects of electromagnetic radiation may subside in the wake of new understanding and modified standards
abstract: A major international controversy has emerged over the biological effects and health hazards of radio-frequency radiation, a term generally taken to mean radiation below the infrared frequency of 300 GHz. It includes electromagnetic radiation ranging from microwave to extremely low frequencies.

articleTitle: Computers: ‘Superpower’ computers: The omnipresent microprocessor can hardly supplant the large high-speed computer in modeling complex systems and phenomena
abstract: The science of computing has advanced tremendously in 30 years, but computing for science is still — relatively — in the Eniac era. Yet, the need for powerful scientific computers is greater than ever. Three-dimensional computer modeling of the world's energy resources, its weather, and its inhabitants has become a major concern of scientists and engineers.

articleTitle: Aerospace: Collision avoidance in space: Proliferating payloads and space debris prompt action to prevent accidents
abstract: Space is infinite; yet the space in Earth's orbit is finite, and collisions in space between man-launched objects have become a threat. As the number and size of orbiting space stations continue to grow, there is increasing danger that they will hit some fragment of “junk” — spent rockets, dead payloads, fragments from explosions and collisions in space, and the like. This “junk” could threaten smaller spacecraft because of the increasing number of fragments from collisions of pieces of debris.

articleTitle: Solid state: Molecular beam epitaxy: Streams of molecules in a vacuum chamber build devices ‘from the atom up’
abstract: Discusses the application of molecular beam epitaxy (MBE), a process for forming thin, single-crystal semiconductor structures in an ultrahigh vacuum. Microwave field-effect transistors, semiconductor lasers, millimeter-wave detectors, and a variety of other high-performance devices have been made from the multilayer crystals grown by the process. With MBE, the thickness of crystalline layers can be precisely controlled down to a few angstroms. Layer composition can be varied, and new semiconductor structures can be produced that are impossible to make by other means. The molecular beams are created when the required elements are heated in effusion ovens-small containers, each with an opening facing the substrate wafer. As many elements and effusion ovens are used as there are elements to be incorporated into the crystal structure. For gallium-arsenide devices, for example, ovens for gallium, for arsenic, and for each of the doping elements are needed.

articleTitle: Computers: Computers that see: Solutions to this difficult challenge may reside in hardware rather than software, or a combination of both
abstract: Computer vision - the automated analysis of visual data - has long been one of the most intractable problems in automation and robotics. While simple types of vision devices, capable of recognizing isolated two-dimensional forms, are now being commercialized, more general vision tasks have remained out of reach. Most researchers in the field believe that the current predominant approach, which regards computer vision as primarily a software problem broadly similar to speech understanding, will eventually achieve useful vision capabilities. However, a growing minority feel that real automated vision will require not just better software, but also hardware that is radically different from present digital computers, hardware more capable of mimicking human vision.

articleTitle: Solid state: VLSI goes to school: In the international struggle for technological leadership, U.S. universities are developing research centers for very-large-scale integrated circuits
abstract: The battlelines for winning the lead in the development of very-large-scale integration have been drawn. The contestants are in the United States, Japan, and Europe. Research is being pressed in the R&D divisions of the U.S. electronics industry and is being spurred by Governmental agencies such as the National Securities Agency, and the Department of Defense and armed services research arms. Increasingly, however, U.S. universities are putting their expertise behind the VLSI effort.

articleTitle: The blue-collar robot: The machine shop and the assembly line will be early beneficiaries of advanced robotic systems
abstract: A customer wishing to have a few gears designed and fabricated walks into a small metalworking shop and hands a rough sketch to a human designer. The designer turns on a graphics terminal connected to a time-sharing network that offers computer-aided design and computer-aided manufacturing capabilities. Using these, the designer designs the gears. If acceptable to the customer, the design program generates control software both for numerical-control cutting machines and for robots to set up and manipulate the parts. Robot conveyors assemble material from bins, and robot machinists then turn out the parts, unattended by any human. Robot vision compares the finished part for tolerance and flaws against master templates generated by the CAD/CAM program. The customer gets the finished parts.

articleTitle: Photovoltaics I: Solar-cell arrays: Clean and silent, solar-cell arrays are targeted to be competitive by 1986
abstract: A general view of the solar power industry briefly mentioning the history and indicating the vast advances made up to the present state-of-the-art in terms of technology and economics. Also indicates the possible contribution of solar-cell produced energy to the overall world demand and consumption provided further economic and technological barriers can be overcome. The research and development at present in the fields of solar cell materials, materials growth and the design of solar-cell arrays at present is indicated and the direction and goals are pointed out.

articleTitle: Solid state looks to VLSI: Meanwhile, uncommitted logic arrays enjoy a revival and new bubble memories are introduced
abstract: The semiconductor industry continued its avowed quest for very-large-scale integration in 1979, generally predicting sample 100 000-gate ram chips sometime this year (vlsi by some definitions) and million-gate chips by the year 2000 (vlsi by any definition).

articleTitle: A computer center for the homeowner
abstract: It is 8 p.m. in the Pearsons' house somewhere in the United States, July 10, 1989. All television sets are on. Mrs. Pearson has selected Category 8 of the information retrieval system, Local Government Services, and is reviewing the schedule of public meetings that will be held during the week. Noticing that the City Council meets tomorrow, she retrieves the minutes of the previous meeting. She could view a video recording if she wished, but she decides to scan through the written minutes and cast her vote now. Later, she has some messages to send.

articleTitle: Crack-detectives foil aircraft failure: Detecting flaws in aircraft is based on nondestructive testing with new interpretive aids on the way
abstract: Anyone who has occupied the window seat of a commercial plane has probably watched the way the wing moves up and down — slowly, like a majestic bird in unhurried flight. This isn't necessarily unnerving, so long as the “flapping” remains reasonable. Aircraft wings are supposed to bend, the way tall buildings sway. If they didn't, they'd break. But when the plane runs into turbulence and the wings start to flutter — you wonder. How much is too much? After ail, metal fatigue is real.

articleTitle: Power/energy: Nuclear waste disposal: Where and how?: How to safely handle one of the most hazardous substances is an urgent problem shared by technologists and the public
abstract: If the radioactive particles in the used nuclear fuel rods from one year's operation of a reactor were to be dispersed in water, it would take all of Lake Superior to dilute them enough so the water would meet U.S. Environmental Protection Agency standards for drinking. The volume of water needed to dilute all used reactor fuel in the U.S. to safe levels would be many times the volume of the world's fresh-water lakes.

articleTitle: Power/energy: Magnetic fusion power: Controlled thermonuclear fusion power using magnetic confinement nows seems practical, but the best method remains uncertain
abstract: Controlled thermonuclear fusion power has long appeared to be the ideal solution to the energy crisis: a source of unlimited, cheap, clean energy whose fuels could be derived from sea water. Yet, the development of fusion power has proved exceedingly difficult, provoking widespread doubt that commercially feasible fusion reactors could be built within the present century. Now, as the result of impressive progress in the last three years, this doubt is evaporating. Scientists both within and outside the fusion research field are confident today that magnetic fields can confine the 100 million-Kelvin plasmas long enough for a reaction and that a demonstration commercial fusion reactor can be built by the year 2000.

articleTitle: New product applications: Universal development system provides real-time emulation from 4 to 32 b at up to 30 MHz
abstract: Universal development system provides real-time emulation from 4 to 32 b at up to 30 MHz: The ECL-3211 provides in-circuit emulation of any microprocessor, from 4 to 32 b, in real time, at speeds up to 30 MHz. Available for stand-alone or down-loaded applications, the microprocessor development system uses a software-driven approach: New emulator hardware does not have to be installed each time a new chip is introduced. The software for the new chip is loaded, and an adapter card is plugged in for the chip family.

articleTitle: Computers: emphasis on software: The microprocessor becomes more versatile while peripheral circuits ‘get smart’
abstract: The microprocessor market is booming, the outlook for mainframes is bullish, and the demand for new software exceeds the supply. And yet, the state of computer technology today recalls the student who complained to the Cambridge philosopher Ludwig Wittgenstein: “I have a problem. I do not feel at home in the universe.”

articleTitle: Technology and policy: Spectrum asks questions of Carter, Reagan, and Anderson: This year's contenders for the U.S. presidency give their views on technology and engineering issues
abstract: Voters in this year's Presidential election can choose among three candidates-President Jimmy Carter on the Democratic line, Ronald Reagan on the Republican, and John li. Anderson, independent - each with different ideas of technology and its place in society. To acquaint readers with their ideas, Spectrum drew up a list of questions and submitted it to each candidate. The topics covered are energy, innovation, productivity, research and development, the space program, defense, pensions for mobile professionals, and engineering and science education. Mr. Carter and Mr. Anderson replied. Ronald Reagan chose not to reply to the questionnaire. Instead, the Reagan stuff supplied official policy statements on a range of topics. In addition, Spectrum received permission from the National Society of Professional Engineers to reprint Mr. Reagan's answers to questions that NSPE submitted to the candidates. These two sources have been used to give readers Mr. Reagan's views on a number of the questions. His views on the rest were unavailable at press time.

articleTitle: Aerospace and military: Space probes score successes; DOD presses high-speed ICs; MLS begins airport tests
abstract: Aerospace and military projects planned early in the 1970s hit paydirt last year, and at least one project that could influence integrated-circuit design through the 1980s got under way. The astounding encounters of Voyager spacecraft with Jupiter and Pioneer spacecraft with Saturn and Venus have led to the redrawing of planetary maps and promise to rewrite theories of the solar system.

articleTitle: New product applications: Digital signal generator has 10 ns resolution up to 100 MHz, and 16 channel operations
abstract: The RS-680 100-MHz digital signal generator may be used as a bench instrument for development applications or as a computer- or calculator-controlled component for use as a synchronizer, modulator, trigger, or gating generator within an automatic test equipment system.

articleTitle: Nuclear power: Mitigating the effects of a nuclear accident: Regulators, states, and utilities argue about distance, time, communication, and who's in charge
abstract: A nationwide effort is under way to generate new plans to protect the public in any future nuclear reactor accident. The Nuclear Regulatory Commission (NRC) and the Federal Emergency Management Agency (FEMA) are urging states and requiring utilities to improve and expand their emergency plans for areas around nuclear power plants. Guidelines issued by the NRC and FEMA are recommending plans for evacuation or sheltering of the public as far as 10 miles (16.1 km) from nuclear plants and for agricultural restrictions as far as 50 miles (80.47 km) out.

articleTitle: Instrumentation: Controlling the synfuel process: Sophisticated electronic instrumentation and safety controls for coal gasification and liquefaction systems are under development
abstract: New approaches to instrumentation are being tried to help control processes in an emerging industry in the United States: the production of synthetic fuels from coal. In converting coal to either gas or liquid, some of the processes create such hostile environments that off-the-shelf instruments operating in them would fail in a short time. Researchers are turning to ultrasonic and capacitive instrumentation and using neutron-induced gamma spectrometry to do the job.

articleTitle: Magnetohydrodynamic power: The road to an operational magnetohydrodynamic power plant is paved with formidable engineering obstacles
abstract: At an engineering test facility in the early 1990s, a 1200-MWt magnetohydrodynamic (MHD) commercial power generator is operating with an overall efficiency of 45 percent. It is delivering electricity at a lower cost than a steam plant, if one takes into account fuel plus operating and maintenance expenses. Energy is being derived from a high-temperature electrically conducting gas. Fueled by coal, the MHD plant is yielding 30 to 50 percent more power from each ton of coal than would a similarly fueled steam plant. The MHD system also emits one-third less SOx, NOx and particulates than a conventional steam plant of a comparable size.

articleTitle: New product applications: IBM-compatible processor provides up to 16 channels and 16 megabytes of main memory
abstract: Advanced System/9000 is a general-purpose processor that provides about twice the instruction execution rates of an IBM 3033 when running identical programs with similar configurations.

articleTitle: Patents: Firmware patents can be firm: Firmware-based inventions may be patentable, but there are traps for the unwary
abstract: More important than the much-argued issue of the patentability of software-based inventions is the patentability of firmware or microprocessor-based inventions. Most software cannot be protected by patent because it lacks the basic requirement of a patentable invention, that of not being obvious. A very complicated program - for example, one which converts Russian to English 6368355 will probably not be patentable, even though its development may have been very laborious and time consuming.

articleTitle: Power/energy developments: High efficiencies and less downtime are sought by utilities as the oil squeeze worsens
abstract: Faced with escalating costs for land, capital, fuel, and labor, power utilities have embarked on a determined effort to get more performance from their equipment at no added cost.

articleTitle: New product applications: S33/A storage-module drive controller is software compatible with DEC RM02 I/O driver
abstract: The S33/A storage-module drive controller for the PDP-11 minicomputers is packaged on a standard Digital Equipment hex board. It is completely software compatible with the RM02 I/O driver and functions with the RSTS/E and RSX11-M operating systems and RM02 diagnostics. It also operates with Control Data Corp.'s 9762 drive and other equivalent storage module drives, including those from Ampex, Ball, and Century Data Systems.

articleTitle: New product applications: Measurement and control link includes 16-b processor and 28-kilobyte user-partitioned RAM
abstract: Measurement and control link includes 16-b processor and 28-kilobyte user-partitioned RAM: The 2400 measurement and control link can be programmed from a host computer to perform a variety of measurements, including temperature, voltage, current, resistance, and pressure. Transducer inputs are converted to engineering units with programmable mathematical functions or up to 12 standard temperature linearizations. The data acquisition device employs a language similar to Basic that is easy to learn and remember. For controlling critical parameters, the 2400A provides such capabilities as programmable voltage, current, resistance, and status.

Waveform recorder can provide up to eight channels of synchronous recording with slave units: The Model 2805 dual-channel waveform recorder comprises a master and up to three slave units. The master unit provides dual-channel recording, with an 8-b word per sample and a maximum 2048-word/channel memory capacity up to 5 MHz. The slave is a master-dependent dual-channel recorder. Used with three slave units, the master can provide up to eight channels of synchronous recording.

articleTitle: New product applications: Digital storage oscilloscope has 10 MHz storage bandwidth and 8-b vertical resolution
abstract: The Model 468 digital storage oscilloscope has all the capabilities of the popular 465B 100-MHz portable oscilloscope in the nonstorage mode. In the storage mode, it continues to operate like a nonstorage oscilloscope. Storage mode is selected by pushing a button; waveforms are acquired and stored as easily as they are viewed in the nonstorage mode.

Note to IEEE Spectrum authors: IEEE Spectrum is the world's largest circulation magazine in the electrical/electronics field; it affords the primary link between the IEEE and all its members. Spectrum objectives are to provide interesting and useful information on a broad range of technical and career-oriented topics and to provide current awareness for its readers of fields outside their immediate specialties. The staff of Spectrum works closely with authors to help them revise their manuscripts, drastically when necessary, to gain high readability and utility to the reader. Spectrum encourages articles of high interest to a large percentage of its readers. Before submitting an article to Spectrum, you may wish to discuss it by telephone with the Editorial Director.

The Eclipse MV/8000 is a state-of-the-art virtual storage 32-b minicomputer based on advanced VLSI technology. It offers a total virtual address space of 4.3 billion bytes and user address spaces of up to 512 megabytes each, a built-in diagnostic processor, a hardware-supported eight-ring security and protection system, and three new 32-b languages.
